en: If anger seizes this poor soul,
I shall gather my white-capped people.
I shall bind the two namesake boys
As a talisman at my waist
And face whatever enemy approaches.
Ah, unfortunate Mother, what are you saying?
Mother, who should hear these words of yours?
Let the sightless night hear them;
Let the towering mountains hear them;
Let the enemy shouting fierce cries
And hollow battle shouts hear them;
Let the dug black grave hear them;
Let the deep earth beneath hear them.
Pretending wisdom, suffering Mother,
You sent my father, now gone to Judgment,
Creeping by day
And whispering by night,
Out on poison raids.
Estranging him from those close to him,
Making him endure countless afflictions,
Mounting him for holy war,
Making him grieve and burn,
You sent him on his way.
My radiant father Manas—
You, Mother, sent him on that road!
My magnanimous father Manas,
Mountainlike as Ala-Too,
You broke and drove from his path,
Turned his mother's kin into enemies,
And brought him to sudden ruin!
Ah, my valiant, unfortunate mother,
You would strip him of mane and tail
And leave him like a wild ass;
Deprive him of walking feet
And leave him like a snake;
Like a stone a hunter casts from a mountain,
You would leave him a stone;
Like something gnawed clean by a ravenous man,
Mother, you would leave him like a bare head.
Bending reason and devising thoughts,
You would turn him into an enemy,
And afterward, upon my head,
Unfortunate Mother, come to no good,
You would raise an enemy!
Upon that sheltering rounded hill
You would raise a mountain;
Upon the head of my closest one
You would raise an enemy.
Do not divide my thoughts;
Do not speak strangely like this
Of the boy who is our support.”
So Semetey spoke.
Though he was khan and lord, he would not listen;
He could not understand Kanchoro’s conduct,
My ill-fated son.
My words meant to calm him
Only brought disgrace upon me.
He called my words corrupt
And put me to shame.
Because of past events,
Because of Kanchoro,
For six months he would not look at me;
When I spoke, he would not heed my words,
Having little trust in me.
He had an amulet hung at his neck,
His grandmother was Chyiyrdy;
He had Chyiyrdy raise him,
With Ajybai carrying him on his back,
And had whatever food he desired given him.
With little trust in his mother,
He had the child's food
Given by Korpeyan.
They fostered and raised him into a hero,
Made him equal to heroes' sons.
When the child reached nine,
They dressed him in flowered silk,
Mounted him on a pacer that led the field,
And took him along to feasts.
They mounted him on an unmatched pacer,
Dressed him in gray almond-patterned cloth,
And taught him openly to rule
The Argyn and Kyrgyz.
They fostered and raised him great,
Made him great among the world's peoples.
When he wept, they comforted him;
When he slept, they woke him;
Leading him with them, they made him a hero,
Equal to heroes' sons.
They joined much that was broken,
Gathered much that was scattered,
Rekindled the extinguished fire,
Brought his dead soul back to life.
They raised him to manhood as a hero,
Made him equal to heroes' sons.
They fed him slices of rich horse meat,
And had him call the bloodthirsty hero his kinsman.
They fed him slices of rich meat
And said that, if he lived,
He would become the hero's support.
To that extraordinary kinsman's child,
I gave my own breast to nurse.
From that day until this,
Whom did he ever call mother?
When bored, he had deer shot;
When roused, he had enemies raided.
This boy he held as his companion—
Look how Kanchoro at last
Became his enemy!
Zulpukor's steel sprang from its sheath;
Conflict came upon Sultan Semetey.
The words this unfortunate woman spoke before
Have now proved true.
He destroyed Beijing and opened a road,
Yet did not fear the spirits.
He slaughtered and disgraced his elder brother.
Ah, my dear child Aichurok,
Do not grieve, my little foal!
Fire sprang from the meadow and burned;
An enemy arose from within.
He poured poison into your vessel;
This Kanchoro here,
My child, has brought you to ruin!
My child, joined iron is not tempered steel;
This raging rabble is not a true people.
Brittle iron is not tempered steel;
Villains raised elsewhere are not your people!
Oh, my little foal Aichurok,
This Keng-Kol is no homeland for you;
In the end Kanchoro is no kin of yours!
Oh, my little foal Aichurok,
My heart is flame, my liver embers.
You bear a six-month child within you.
I place my hope in God;
My heart rests in the Creator.
My child Aichurok, seeing humiliation
And hardship,
I shall weep and burn with you.
For exactly twelve years
I shall mourn for you!
Until twelve years have passed,
I shall live enduring humiliation.
If you do not return in twelve years,
I shall die in lamentation.
Oh, my little foal Aichurok,
You were a master of wisdom.
If the gift in your womb
Is a girl rather than a boy,
My child Aichurok, send a letter;
When you send it, send it swiftly!
I shall braid the hair down my back;
Burning and smoldering like an ember,
I, Kanykei, shall die that day.
But if it is a son,
Hold his full celebration
And name him Seitek!
Hang a sign around his neck;
Raise him without dressing him in dirty clothes,
Without feeding him tainted food,
Without letting filth touch him!
My child, see how his grandfather's
Valor follows from his father!
When he reaches thirteen,
Tell him of Zhylgyndy and Keng-Kol,
Tell him of the joyous Kyrgyz people;
Tell him of river-rich Talas,
Tell him of the Argyn and Kyrgyz;
Tell him all the abundant wonders;
Tell him of me, the fierce, bereaved woman!
Oh, my dear Aichurok,
Silk does not fade into sackcloth;
My good woman, my little foal,
A noble woman captured by foes does not become a slave.
Bind on courage and act like a lion.
Your kin have become your enemies;
Your adversary is within.
My child, show courage now.
Oh, my little foal Aichurok,
Know and remember what I have said.
When Allah lays a burden on us,
There is no choice but to bear it.
Oh, Aichurok, heed my words.
Kulchoro has gone into captivity;
My foal may have died in misery!
If he is still alive,
He must be enduring humiliation.
Though a hero and a lion,
He has become a herdsman's slave,
His collarbone rubbed raw,
Both his hands aching,
Wearing a coat that keeps him alive,
Drinking water that keeps his spark from dying,
Burning and glowing like an ember,
Scorched to ashes,
My Kulchoro must live in anguish!
If you do not watch over him, it will bring disgrace;
Kulchoro is entrusted to you!
See his eyes each year;
When his felt coat tears,
Oh, my little foal Aichurok,
Patch it for him from time to time.
If he grows hungry, feed him;
Your younger brother Kulchoro—
If he grows thin, fatten him.
If you do not watch over him, it will bring disgrace.
Oh, my little foal Aichurok,
Kulchoro is entrusted to you!"
So Kanykei spoke,
Your dear, unfortunate mother,
At times grieving, at times weeping,
Urging her toward lionhearted courage.
At times lamenting, at times weeping,
She urged her toward heroic resolve.
Before she had closed her mouth,
Before she could finish every word,
May God never show such a sight!
The battle standard surged like a flag;
A din arose that split the sky.
A vast army flooded forth,
Firing cannon and drawing bows,
And covered the road.
They encircled the palace amid uproar;
A din arose that split the sky.
Spearheads clashed,
And all the champions raced forward.
Dust flew into the sky;
The army spread in a dusty glitter.
They advanced with battle-axes in hand,
Swords striking from their sheaths.
Their divisions split and opened,
Their multitude plain to the people.
They were many tens of thousands,
An army by no means small.
The people bustled and dust swirled;
They seemed to fill the face of the world.
The layered black earth below
Smoked thickly
Beneath Kanchoro's wrath.
The earth turned gray amid clamor;
A din arose that split the sky.
Haze spread and darkened it.
The multitude of Zhediger
Flooded over the land
Until they seemed one with the earth.
The cunning and the mighty,
Those who broke ranks with spears,
Met the men of the gate;
Those whose death had come fell to bullets.
Shouting the cry, "Kanchoro Khan!"
The furious myriad army
Raised the battle cry, "Kiyaz!"
They flew in like flies,
Surrounded them, writhing like worms,
And streamed like ants.
The gatekeepers and Zhediger
Stood facing one another,
Firing cannon and bows,
